title: Can You Marry Someone You Don't Feel "In Love" With?
paragraphs:
Can You Marry Someone You Don't Feel "In Love" With?
The Question That Could Save You from the Greatest Mistake of Your Life—or Lead You to the Greatest Love You Never Expected
What if the biggest lie about marriage isn't that love doesn't exist... but that we've completely misunderstood what love actually is?
What if the butterflies that make your heart race today disappear five years from now?
What if the person who gives you goosebumps isn't the one who will still be holding your hand when life shatters your dreams?
What if the person God is preparing for you doesn't make your emotions explode... but makes your soul become more like Christ?
That question has quietly haunted countless Christians.
"Can I marry someone I don't feel 'in love' with?"
Some are terrified because they care deeply for someone, admire their character, enjoy being with them, trust them completely, and know they would make an incredible husband or wife...
...yet they don't feel the overwhelming emotional fireworks everyone keeps talking about.
Others feel trapped because they're chasing a feeling that never stays.
Hollywood says, "Follow your heart."
Scripture quietly asks something far more dangerous.
"Whose heart?"
Because the Bible says:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9, ESV)

The Hebrew word translated "deceitful" is עָקֹב (ʿāqōḇ), carrying the idea of something crooked, insidious, unreliable, or treacherous. It is not saying that emotions are evil; rather, it warns that our fallen hearts are not trustworthy guides apart from God's truth.
That changes everything.
From the very beginning, God never described marriage as the climax of romantic feelings.
Genesis tells us:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." (Genesis 2:24)

The Hebrew expression וְדָבַק (wəḏāḇaq), translated "hold fast" or "cleave," literally means to cling, to stick, to remain firmly attached. It describes covenantal commitment before it describes emotional excitement.
Marriage begins with covenant.
Feelings may accompany it.
Feelings may even grow because of it.
But feelings were never designed to sustain it.
One of the greatest misunderstandings in modern Christianity is confusing infatuation with biblical love.
The New Testament repeatedly uses the Greek word ἀγάπη (agapē) when speaking about the highest form of love.
Agapē is not primarily a feeling.
It is a self-giving, sacrificial commitment seeking another person's good.
Paul defines it in 1 Corinthians 13:

"Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way... Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends."
Notice something astonishing.
Paul never mentions butterflies.
He never mentions chemistry.
He never mentions emotional intensity.
Instead, love is described as deliberate action flowing from transformed character.
This doesn't mean emotions are unimportant.
God created emotions.
Jesus Himself wept.
Jesus rejoiced.
Jesus loved deeply.
But Jesus never allowed emotions to become His highest authority.
He always submitted His desires to His Father's will.
That is the pattern for every Christian relationship.
Can you marry someone you don't feel "in love" with?
The better question is this:
What exactly do you mean by "in love"?
If you mean you feel absolutely nothing...
No affection.
No admiration.
No attraction whatsoever.
No desire to build a life together.
Then wisdom says you should slow down.
Marriage is not merely a duty.
Song of Songs celebrates delight between husband and wife.
Physical attraction matters.
Friendship matters.
Joy matters.
Desire matters.
God invented them.
They are gifts.
But if by "not in love" you simply mean you don't experience overwhelming emotional highs every moment...
You are describing nearly every healthy marriage at different seasons.
Emotions rise.
Emotions fall.
Commitment remains.
Many couples who have walked faithfully with Christ for decades will tell you something surprising.
The deepest love often came after the wedding.
Not before it.
Trust was built.
Forgiveness was practiced.
Children were raised.
Hospital rooms were visited.
Bills were paid.
Prayers were answered.
Tears were shared.
Scars became testimonies.
And somewhere along the way...
Love became deeper than romance ever promised.
The world tells you to marry because you're overwhelmed by feelings.
The Bible teaches you to marry because you've wisely discerned godly character, mutual commitment, covenant readiness, and genuine affection under God's guidance.
Ephesians 5 points us to the ultimate model.
"Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." (Ephesians 5:25)
The Greek phrase παρέδωκεν ἑαυτόν (paredōken heauton) means "gave Himself over." Christ's love is measured not by emotional intensity but by sacrificial surrender.
Jesus did not go to the cross because Calvary felt pleasant.
Hebrews reminds us that He endured the cross for the joy set before Him.
Love acts.
Love sacrifices.
Love remains.
That is why biblical marriage is so much bigger than romance.
It is a living sermon about the Gospel itself.
Every faithful husband whispers something about Christ.
Every faithful wife reflects something about the Church.
Marriage was never designed to worship itself.
Marriage points beyond itself.
It points to Jesus.
Some readers may be carrying another question.
"What if I once felt deeply in love... but I don't anymore?"
Take heart.
Feelings can return.
Sometimes they return through repentance.
Sometimes through forgiveness.
Sometimes through intentional kindness.
Sometimes through healing wounds that were never addressed.
Sometimes after years of faithfully choosing one another.
Love often grows where selfishness dies.
That is one reason Scripture commands husbands to love.
Commands are given because love is not merely accidental emotion.
It is Spirit-enabled obedience.
This also protects us from another danger.
Never marry someone simply because they are "nice" while ignoring serious biblical concerns.
Do they genuinely follow Christ?
Do they display the fruit of the Spirit?
Can they repent?
Can they forgive?
Are they trustworthy?
Are they teachable?
Do they honor God's Word?
These questions matter far more than whether your pulse quickens every time they walk into the room.
Butterflies cannot carry a marriage through suffering.
Character can.
The Gospel reminds us that none of us entered a relationship with Jesus because we deserved His affection.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice the order.
Christ's covenant love came before our transformation.
His love changed us.
It did not wait for us to become lovable.
Marriage cannot imitate the Gospel perfectly.
But it reflects its shape.
A covenant sustained by grace.
A love strengthened by sacrifice.
A commitment renewed through forgiveness.
That is why our ministry exists under one simple theme:
Every believer carries a story stained by sin, disappointment, fear, regret, failure, broken expectations, or shattered dreams.
Yet Jesus is still writing.
He still restores.
He still redeems.
He still transforms ordinary people into extraordinary testimonies of His grace.
Perhaps today you are waiting for perfect certainty before saying yes to someone who genuinely loves Christ.
Perhaps you are chasing emotions while overlooking godly character.
Or perhaps you are already married and wondering whether your love story is beyond repair.
The cross answers every one of those fears.
Because the greatest love story in history was never built on changing feelings.
It was built on an unchanging Savior.
If this article challenged something you've believed for years, don't rush past it.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers.
Let God's Word—not culture, social media, movies, or fleeting emotions—shape your understanding of marriage.
Share what God taught you, or simply comment, "Jesus, teach me to love the way You love." Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
Your support enables us to continue producing Christ-centered articles, devotionals, biblical studies, Gospel resources, and discipleship content that points people to Jesus instead of trends.
Because one shared article can reach a wandering son.
One act of faithfulness can echo into eternity.
And perhaps the greatest love story you will ever witness... is not the one that begins at the altar, but the one that began at the cross.
